theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Arrays, Functions and Command Lines

The C standard defines the subscript operator through pointer arithmetic: E1[E2] means *((E1) + (E2)). An array name decays to a pointer to its first element in every expression except when it is the operand of sizeof or of unary &, so a[i], *(a + i), *(i + a) and even i[a] name the same element. Decay keeps the address but fixes the type, and the type decides how far + 1 moves. That is why a, &a[0] and &a all start at the same byte, yet a + 1 and &a + 1 land in different places.

theoryAdd.plainText: address of m[i][j] = base B + (i × C + j) × sizeof(T), where C is the number of columns (row-major)

theoryAdd.text: To read a declaration, start at the name, look right for [ ] or ( ), then look left for *, and let parentheses override that order. Because [ ] and ( ) bind more tightly than *, int *p[4] is an array of 4 pointers, while int (*p)[4] is a single pointer to an array of 4 ints. The same rule separates int *f(int), a function returning int *, from int (*f)(int), a pointer to such a function.

Mistakes and special cases to watch for:
items: A function that swaps its pointer parameters (int *t = x; x = y; y = t;) changes only its own copies; a real swap exchanges *x and *y.
A 2-D array does not convert to int **. Pass it to int m[][4] or int (*m)[4], because the column count is part of the type.
A pointer may walk from a up to a + n (one past the end) but no further, and never down to a − 1; write reverse loops so that the pointer stops at a instead of stepping below it.
char *s = "abc" points at a read-only literal, while char s[] = "abc" is a writable 4-byte copy; sizeof gives the pointer size for the first and 4 for the second.
A qsort comparator written as return x - y; can overflow when the values are far apart; return (x > y) - (x < y); is always safe.
atoi(argv[i]) returns 0 for text that is not a number, so validate the input (or use strtol) before trusting the value.

theoryAdd.text: Rewrite every expression into pure pointer form before evaluating it: x[i] becomes *(x + i), x[i][j] becomes *(*(x + i) + j), and argv[i][j] becomes *(*(argv + i) + j). Then ask what type each step has: stepping a row pointer skips a whole row, while stepping an element pointer skips one element.

questions.explanation: An array name is not a modifiable lvalue, so it can never be assigned to (a = r, a++). The other statements store addresses in the pointer variable p, which is legal; a + 4 is the address of the last element.

options: Compile error: 2[a] is not valid C
questions.explanation: E1[E2] is defined as *((E1) + (E2)) and addition is commutative, so 2[a] = *(2 + a) = a[2] = 12 and 1[a] = a[1] = 8. Then *(a + 3) − 1[a] = 16 − 8 = 8.

questions.questionText: Inside main, where int a[8]; is declared, which expression gives the number of elements of a (8)?
questions.explanation: sizeof a is the size of the whole array (8 × sizeof(int)) and sizeof a[0] is one element, so the quotient is 8. The trick works only where a is the array itself, not a pointer parameter.

questions.questionText: For int a[10]; int *p = a; which statement is TRUE?
options: a can be incremented with a++ just like p
a and &a hold the same address value but have different types
questions.explanation: a (decayed to &a[0]) and &a start at the same byte, but a is int * while &a is int (*)[10], so with 4-byte ints a + 1 moves 4 bytes and &a + 1 moves 40. sizeof a is the size of the whole array (10 × sizeof(int), 40 bytes with 4-byte ints), not a pointer size, and an array name cannot be incremented.
*a + 1 is (*a) + 1 = 7 + 1 = 8, because unary * binds tighter than +. *(a + 1) is a[1] = 2, and 2 + a[3] = 2 + 4 = 6.
p visits a[0], a[2] and a[4] (5, 4 and 3) and stops when it reaches a + 6, the one-past-the-end address, so s = 12.

questions.questionText: What does the declaration int (*p)[5]; declare?
options: An array of 5 pointers to int
A function that returns a pointer to int
A pointer to an array of 5 ints
A pointer to a pointer to int
questions.explanation: The parentheses bind * to p first, so p is a pointer, and what it points to is [5] of int, a whole array. Without them, int *p[5] would be an array of 5 int pointers.
a is an array of 5 pointers: 5 × 8 = 40 bytes. b is a single pointer (8 bytes), and *b is the array of 5 ints it points to: 5 × 4 = 20 bytes.
r points to whole rows of 2 ints, so r++ moves it to m[1]. (*r)[1] is m[1][1] = 4, and r[1] is the next row m[2], so r[1][0] = 5.
p points to w[1], so **p is 'g'. *(p + 1) is w[2], the string "blue", and *(*p + 2) is w[1][2], the 'e' of "green".
After pp++, pp points to p[1], which holds a + 2, so **pp = 30 and *(*pp + 1) = a[3] = 40. pp + 2 is &p[3], which holds a, so **(pp + 2) + 1 = 10 + 1 = 11.
*(*(m + 2) + 1) is m[2][1] = 2 and *(m[1] + 3) is m[1][3] = 1. **m is m[0][0] = 12, and the + 5 is added to that value, giving 17.

sum adds the elements from b up to, but not including, e. sum(a, a + 6) covers a[0] to a[5]: 3 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 5 + 9 = 23, and sum(a + 2, a + 4) covers a[2] and a[3]: 4 + 1 = 5. The end pointer a + 6 points one past the last element, which may be formed and compared but is never dereferenced.
m decays to a pointer to a row of 5 ints, so m + 1 is 20 bytes further on. *m is row 0 decayed to int *, so *m + 1 is 4 bytes on, and &m points to the whole 3 × 5 array, so &m + 1 is 60 bytes on.

questions.questionText: main declares int m[3][4]; and calls f(m, 3);. Which prototype for f is correct?
questions.explanation: Only the first dimension may be omitted, because the compiler needs the column count to locate m[i][j]; int m[][4] means int (*m)[4]. m does not convert to int **, since it decays to a pointer to an array of 4 ints.
*(*(m + i) + i) is m[i][i], so the function adds the main diagonal: 1 + 5 + 9 = 15.

options: Compile error: pointer parameters cannot be reassigned
questions.explanation: swapp exchanges only its own copies of the two addresses and never dereferences them, so a and b are untouched. A working swap must exchange *x and *y.

lo and hi are passed by address, so stats writes its results straight into them: the smallest element is −2 and the largest is 9. Output parameters like these let a C function return more than one value.
f receives the address of a[1], so p[0], p[1] and p[2] are a[1], a[2] and a[3], which gain 0, 1 and 2. The changes appear in main's array because only the address was copied.

questions.questionText: Why is the & needed in scanf("%d", &n); when n is an int?
options: & converts the typed characters into an int
& tells scanf that n is a global variable
& is needed only because n has not been initialised yet
scanf must receive n's address so that it can store the value in the caller's variable
questions.explanation: C passes arguments by value, so scanf could not change n if it received only n's value. Given &n, it writes the converted number through the pointer; an array name such as a char buffer is already an address and needs no &.

questions.questionText: What does const guarantee in the prototype void print(const int *a, int n);?
options: a cannot be moved (a++ is illegal) inside print
The caller may pass only an array that is declared const
print cannot modify the array elements through a
n also becomes read-only inside print
questions.explanation: const int *a is a pointer to read-only ints: a[i] = 0 inside print is a compile error, but a itself may be incremented. An ordinary int array can still be passed to it.

questions.questionText: Which function returns a pointer that the caller can safely use after the call?
questions.explanation: A static local lives for the whole run of the program, so its address stays valid. The automatic x and a are destroyed when f returns (leaving dangling pointers), and the last version writes through an uninitialised pointer.
The strict > keeps the first maximum, so largest returns &v[1] and p − v = 1. *p = 0 writes into v itself, making v[1] = 0 while v[3] stays 8.
Both calls return the address of the same static c, which is 10 after the second call, so p == q is 1. *p += 1 makes c 11, and *p and *q both read 11.
find returns a pointer to the first 'w', which is t + 3. Printing that pointer with %s shows the rest of the string, "work", and p − t = 3.

questions.questionText: Which declaration makes fp a pointer to a function that takes two ints and returns an int?
questions.explanation: The parentheses make fp a pointer first, and the (int, int) after them says it points to a function. int *fp(int, int) declares a function returning int *, and int (*fp)[2] is a pointer to an array.
op first points to add, so r = 5. After op = mul, (*op)(2, 2) = 4 and op(5, 4) = 20; op(...) and (*op)(...) are two spellings of the same call.
f is an array of three function pointers called in order: inc(3) = 4, dbl(4) = 8 and sqr(8) = 64.
qsort calls cmp back to order the elements by their distance from 5: 5 (0), 6 (1), 8 (3), 1 (4) and 12 (7). All the distances differ, so the order is fully determined.

questions.questionText: In the call qsort(v, n, sizeof v[0], cmp); the function cmp is best described as:
options: A recursive function that calls itself to sort the array
An inline function that the compiler pastes into the source of qsort
A macro that the preprocessor expands before compilation
A callback: qsort receives its address and calls it whenever two elements must be compared
questions.explanation: The name cmp decays to a function pointer that qsort stores and calls back as needed. This lets one library sorting routine work with any element type and any ordering.
twice applies g two times: sub3(sub3(10)) = 10 − 3 − 3 = 4, and neg(neg(7)) = 7.

questions.questionText: Given int f(int); and int (*fp)(int);, which statement is correct?
options: Only fp = &f; is legal, because a function name is not an address
fp = f; and fp = &f; are equivalent, and fp(3) and (*fp)(3) both call f
fp(3) is illegal; a function pointer must always be called as (*fp)(3)
fp++ makes fp point to the next function defined in the file
questions.explanation: A function name decays to a pointer to the function, so the & is optional, and a call through the pointer may be written with or without the explicit *. Arithmetic such as fp++ is not allowed on function pointers in standard C (GCC accepts it only as an extension that steps 1 byte, never to another function).
*(s + 2) is s[2] = 'C'. s + 4 is the address of the 'N', and %s prints from there up to the terminator: "NSE".
p stops at the first '\0', so p − s is the number of characters before it: 4 for "exam". In "ab\0cd" the embedded '\0' ends the scan after 2 characters.
a is a 6-byte array holding the 5 letters and the '\0'. p is only a pointer (8 bytes), and strlen counts the 5 characters before the terminator.
The loop copies every character including the terminating '\0'. The second call writes 'k' into buf[3] and '\0' into buf[4], so the string now ends after "poik" and its length is 4.

questions.questionText: In C, what is the effect of the statements char *s = "abc"; s[0] = 'x';?
options: s now points to the string "xbc"
A compile error in every C compiler
Undefined behaviour, because a string literal must not be modified
Only a private copy changes, and the literal itself stays "abc"
questions.explanation: s points directly at the string literal, which may be stored in read-only memory, so writing to it is undefined and often crashes. char s[] = "abc"; makes a modifiable array copy instead.
hi starts at s[3], so only the first four characters are reversed: s[0] is swapped with s[3] and s[1] with s[2], after which lo > hi. s[4] = 'E' is never touched.

questions.questionText: A program declared with int main(int argc, char *argv[]) is run as: prog alpha beta. What is the value of argc?
questions.explanation: argc counts the program name too: argv[0] is the program name, argv[1] is "alpha" and argv[2] is "beta", so argc = 3.
argc is 4 (the program name plus three words), so argv[argc − 1] is argv[3] = "blue". argv[1] is "red", and argv[1][1] is its second character, 'e'.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the parameters of int main(int argc, char *argv[]) is correct?
options: argv[0] is always the first argument typed after the program name
argc counts only the arguments that follow the program name
The elements of argv are ints, so they can be used in arithmetic directly
questions.explanation: The C standard guarantees that argv[argc] is a null pointer, so argv can be walked until NULL. argv[0] is the program name and argc includes it, and every element is a string (char *) that needs atoi or strtol before arithmetic.

options: The program stops with a run-time error at "x"
questions.explanation: argc is 5 (sum, 10, 20, x and 5). atoi returns 0 for text that does not begin with a number, so s = 10 + 20 + 0 + 5 = 35.

questions.questionText: Which is a standard way to declare main so that it receives command-line arguments?
questions.explanation: The standard form is int main(int argc, char *argv[]), and char **argv is the same parameter type because an array parameter is adjusted to a pointer. The count comes first, and argv is an array of strings, not of single chars.

questions.questionText: Compare char a[3][10] = {"Ram", "Sita", "Hari"}; with char *b[3] = {"Ram", "Sita", "Hari"};. Which statement is correct?
options: a and b always occupy exactly the same amount of memory
b[1][0] = 'G'; is safe, but a[1][0] = 'G'; is a compile error
a reserves 30 bytes of writable characters, while b holds 3 pointers to string literals that must not be modified
sizeof b is 30, the same as sizeof a
questions.explanation: a is a true 2-D array: each of its 3 rows has 10 chars (30 bytes) copied from the literals, and they may be edited. b is an array of 3 pointers (3 × pointer size) aimed at read-only literals, so writing b[1][0] is undefined behaviour.
m + 1 points to row m[1], so inside bump r[0] is m[1] and r[1] is m[2]. r[0][0] (m[1][0]) becomes 40 and r[1][1] (m[2][1]) becomes 80, while m[1][1] stays 5.

questions.questionText: In a program with int main(int argc, char *argv[]), which expression is equivalent to argv[2][0]?
questions.explanation: Applying x[i] ≡ *(x + i) twice gives argv[2][0] = *(*(argv + 2) + 0) = **(argv + 2), the first character of the third string. *(*argv + 2) is argv[0][2], and *(argv + 2) is the string pointer argv[2], not a char.
